title: Leading with Proof: IonQ’s Blueprint for Quantum-Safe Enterprise Security
summary: IonQ has devised a quantum-safe security solution leveraging the strengths of both quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
body_markdown:
*At a glance:*


● *IonQ has devised a quantum-safe security solution leveraging the strengths of both quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC).*


● *This hybrid approach is now running live in IonQ’s own network, protecting the company’s mission-critical data between locations in Geneva, Switzerland, and Seoul, South Korea.*


● *IonQ is showing organizations how they can act now to accelerate their own quantum-safe security migrations, and mitigate the risk of “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” attacks.*


● *The solution directly addresses recent proclamations by governments worldwide urging more rapid migration to quantum-safe security.*


● *The hybrid solution is just one aspect of IonQ’s broader roadmap to help organizations worldwide reduce their exposure to threats that could cause revenue loss and weaken operational stability.*


## Hybrid QKD+PQC Approach Adds a New Layer of Protection as Q-Day Nears


IonQ today has a multi-layered approach ready to help corporate and government organizations prepare for the imminent cybersecurity threat posed by near-term quantum computers. This global, hybrid quantum-safe security initiative, leveraging both quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) technologies, is deployed now on a portion of IonQ’s network between Switzerland and South Korea, and is protecting IonQ’s own valuable assets.


Our intent in highlighting our own deployment is to show government leaders and corporate executives everywhere the action they can–and must–take right now to reduce susceptibility to quantum attacks and their consequences–huge financial losses, damage to critical infrastructure and operations, and great harm to brand reputation and organizational stability.


We have been living for decades with the knowledge that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could one day crack public-key cryptography algorithms like Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). In 1994, Peter Shor developed Shor’s Algorithm, which could be run on a quantum computer to efficiently factorize large numbers. Since factoring is the mathematical problem underlying both RSA and ECC, this means a quantum computer of the right size could break both schemes. No such quantum machine existed back then, but the knowledge that one eventually would exist led to that line on the horizon being called “Q-Day.”


More than 30 years later, there is new urgency about Q-Day, in large part because quantum computing capabilities are advancing more quickly than ever. IonQ’s[early benchmarking](https://investors.ionq.com/news/news-details/2019/IonQ-publishes-new-benchmarks-for-quantum-computation/default.aspx) of a quantum computer’s ability to run advanced algorithms, and our[achievement of Algorithmic Qubit goals ahead of schedule](https://www.ionq.com/blog/ionq-hits-aq-64-milestone-ahead-of-schedule-and-sets-its-sights-even-higher) are just two proof points of this acceleration. Error mitigation and correction capabilities also have evolved quickly, enabling quantum computers to more efficiently translate physical qubits into logical qubits that could achieve algorithm runs with greater efficiency and accuracy.


These achievements compressed the Q-Day timeline. It was once thought that millions of qubits would be required to crack RSA and ECC, but recent research suggests the necessary number could be much smaller. Last March, Google Quantum AI and its research partners[published a landmark whitepaper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28846) claiming 256-bit ECC could be broken with as few as 1,200 logical qubits drawn from a quantum machine capable of 500,000 physical qubits. This research drove Google to urge[migration to PQC](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/cryptography-migration-timeline/) by 2029. Other research has suggested that[fewer than 100,000 qubits](https://thequantuminsider.com/2026/02/13/new-architecture-could-cut-quantum-hardware-needed-to-break-rsa-2048-by-tenfold-study-finds/) could be required to factor a 2,048-bit RSA integer. Yet another paper, from researchers at Caltech and Oratomic, claimed Shor’s Algorithm could be run[with as few as 10,000 qubits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28627) .


But, here’s the most urgent reality check about Q-Day: By the time quantum computers can run Shor’s Algorithm, it will be too late for corporations and governments to begin adopting quantum-safe security. Migrating to this new layer of protection can take an organization several years, including laborious and time-consuming enterprise-wide asset inventories, vendor selection processes, and testing and validation phases. To put it simply, organizations can’t wait any longer to start down this road.


Hackers certainly aren’t waiting. The world has come to a queasy understanding that they could be stealing encrypted data right now, and planning to use a quantum computer later to break the locks–a practice commonly known as “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” (HNDL).


IonQ’s proactive effort to strengthen IT security practices reflects this reality, and also arrives as nations around the world are coming to terms with the quantum threat. For example, in the US, a new mandate recently pulled forward the deadlines for federal government agencies to adopt PQC-standard public keys and quantum-safe digital signatures. Meanwhile, in Europe, the European Commission recently said all member states should start transitioning to PQC[by the end of this year](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/eu-reinforces-its-cybersecurity-post-quantum-cryptography) . The governments of the US and Japan also recently agreed to[“collaborate to accelerate”](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/07/joint-statement-of-the-united-states-and-japan-on-cybersecurity-cooperation) PQC adoption in their respective countries.


All of the above make the quantum threat a present and practical corporate risk management and governance priority for government agencies, corporate boards and C-level officers worldwide.


## A Pragmatic Enterprise Defense Solution


This encroaching reality and new sense of urgency set the stage for IonQ’s new hybrid protection architecture that encompasses both QKD and PQC in a single infrastructure solution to help protect widely distributed corporate and government locations.


This infrastructure is operational now in its inaugural deployment across two continents, securing four IonQ sites between Geneva, Switzerland, and Seoul, South Korea. In this new hybrid approach, QKD protects local fiber links connecting IonQ sites in Geneva, providing information-theoretic security for high-priority internal communications, while an additional layer of PQC secures software-defined VPN endpoints between Geneva and IonQ’s South Korea headquarters.


This deployment is not a standalone project, but the first step in a broader global program that has been undertaken by IonQ to provide a blueprint for executing a systematic, scalable, and repeatable strategy for implementing quantum-safe security.


A closer look at QKD and PQC:


QKD PQC


Transmission of encryption keys over a network, secured by quantum principles. Math-based public-key algorithms built on lattice structures and multi-variate equations, thought to be resilient against quantum computers.


Local QKD networks are already deployed, with many more to come, and eventually longer-distance QKD links with satellites or quantum networks. Can be installed quickly and widely on servers, VPNs, smartphones, computers, and IoT devices.


Keeps the public-key infrastructure used today to secure the Internet.


Communication between QKD and encryption systems and a Protection Profile for QKD devices standardized by ETSI. Standardized by NIST, endorsed by US CISA.


Not susceptible to future mathematical breakthroughs. Security relies on computational hardness assumptions — resilience against future quantum and AI attacks continues to be actively researched and validated.


Limited to fixed connectivity, with optical fibers or free space.


Not easily applicable to temporary connections. Hybrid architecture ensures PQC continuity even if a QKD intermediate relay node is compromised, though this will not be an issue in the future quantum networks.


Together, QKD and PQC offer thorough quantum-safe security that no single technology can provide on its own, and IonQ has them working in concert now in a live deployment. This is not a sandbox deployment or a field trial; this is IonQ using its long-tested, proven, and validated quantum-safe security techniques on its own mission-critical, international infrastructure to add new layers of security onto its enterprise defenses.


## Proving by Using


The growing sense of urgency around Q-Day has fostered a market for quantum-safe security solutions that is full of noise and unproven vendor promises. Enterprise buyers might be pressured into choosing one security technology over others depending on who is making the case, and require lengthy trial periods to determine what works and what doesn’t.


By using this hybrid quantum-safe security approach on IonQ’s own live infrastructure, and entrusting it to protect its own crown jewels—proprietary research data and intellectual property—IonQ is proving to corporate and government leaders that they can trust this QKD+PQC solution to secure their own mission-critical data. We are cutting through the noise to present them with a path they can choose now to strengthen their own enterprise security defenses.


IonQ is uniquely positioned to do so, as it is not just a quantum computing hardware manufacturer, but the only company vertically integrating quantum computing hardware, quantum sensing, quantum networking, quantum memory research, and quantum-safe security techniques under one roof. IonQ also is among a very small number of organizations globally—and the only quantum computing company—to operate a live hybrid QKD+PQC network on its own international infrastructure.


In addition, IonQ separately has deployed QKD networks across government and financial sectors worldwide. Plus, in other previous projects separate from this new initiative, we worked with partners like EPB Quantum at a[quantum networking and QKD hub in Chattanooga, Tennessee](https://www.ionq.com/news/ionq-announces-usd22m-deal-with-epb-establishing-chattanooga-tennessee-as) , to advance how quantum keys can be distributed over fiber networks. IonQ also has aligned QKD and PQC in its[Clavis and Clarion product lines](https://www.ionq.com/news/ionq-introduces-clavis-xg-multiplex-making-quantum-security-deployable-at-scale-in-metro-networks) .


## Mitigating the HNDL Risk


IonQ’s vertically integrated assets and expertise in quantum-safe security can now be merged with everything government and corporate technology leaders already have learned about how to best protect their enterprises from cybersecurity threats.


These leaders have long understood that there has never been and there will never be one magical security solution that can beat back all attacks. The cybersecurity threat landscape continues to become sophisticated at every turn, and the best defense an organization has is to create layers of different kinds of protection, and continually update and add to these layers as often as possible. QKD and PQC represent the latest layers ready to be added to enterprise defense programs.


As noted earlier, hackers deploying HNDL schemes do not even need to wait for Q-Day. That means any organizations with assets and data they deem worth protecting from the quantum threat must face the sobering responsibility to adopt a quantum-safe layer now to reduce their risk of being affected by HNDL attacks. Acting now could even help defuse the HNDL threat to some degree as quantum-safe security becomes more widely adopted across industries.


## The Roadmap to a More Secure Enterprise.


This new hybrid QKD+PQC infrastructure is just one step in a Full Quantum Convergence roadmap that will help enable more secure enterprises worldwide. For example, we are planning to eventually deploy the hybrid infrastructure at IonQ’s corporate headquarters in College Park, Maryland. The roadmap will take us from fiber-based QKD networks today to satellite-based QKD, which will help QKD scale globally, and eventually further in the future to quantum repeaters that will enable future quantum networks. These quantum networks will remove the limitation of trusted nodes and provide end-to-end secure key distribution over long distances. They will use the technology developed by IonQ in our trapped ion processors and quantum memories, further exemplifying the value of IonQ’s vertically-integrated full stack approach.


But, back to the present. The migration to a quantum-safe security posture cannot be deferred until Q-Day arrives. Recent acceleration toward fault-tolerant quantum computing and rapidly advancing error mitigation and logical qubit achievements have highlighted the growing sense of urgency with which government and corporate enterprise leaders must act. The time to begin implementing hybrid architectures is now. IonQ leads with proof, not promises, and our new hybrid QKD+PQC solution is that proof.
